extracted.intended_audience: readers of political economy; policymakers, administrators, and merchants interested in public works and commercial institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding who should fund, manage, and regulate public works and commercial protections (central government, local/provincial bodies, or merchant companies), and how different company forms affect trade, governance, and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs central management of small/public-district works
rubrics_metrics.description: Even public works whose convenience is nearly confined to some particular place or district are always better maintained by a local or provincial revenue, under the management of a local and provincial administration, than by the general revenue of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: London streets would not be as well lit and paved if paid from the national treasury — expense would be borne by all inhabitants though most do not benefit. Local funding ties costs to beneficiaries, reduces waste and mis-prioritization. Watch for central neglect of many small but useful works and the unfair spread of taxation when benefits are localized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central administration favors grand, visible works
rubrics_metrics.description: High-visibility projects (great highways, works seen by principal nobility) attract central ministers who seek splendour and public applause; small but extremely useful works are neglected as 'too mean and paltry'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: ministers prefer projects that flatter vanity or are visible to elites. Evaluate whether central sponsorship is driven by public need or by vanity and political spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of sovereign revenue sources with management incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Where sovereign revenue arises from land tax (as in China/parts of Asia), the sovereign's revenue is immediately connected to cultivation and to providing extensive, cheap communications (roads/canals); thus executive power attends to such public works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the state's revenue structure aligns its incentives with maintaining infrastructure. If revenue depends on land produce, central interest in roads/canals rises; if revenue is diverse (as in much of Europe), central motivation weakens and local management may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local abuses vs empire-level administration risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses in local/provincial administration, however enormous they may appear, are almost always very trifling in comparison to those in administration and expenditure of a great empire's revenue and are much more easily corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the scale and correctability of abuses: prefer decentralized options when their abuses are smaller and easier to remediate than systemic central mismanagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding extraordinary protection for particular branches of commerce by specific taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary expenses for protecting particular branches of commerce should be defrayed by a moderate tax upon that particular branch (e.g., a fine upon entering the trade or a particular per-cent duty on goods), rather than by general taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of beneficiary-pays: protection costs that serve a particular trade ought to be charged to that trade. Example: duties of customs originally arose to protect trade generally; similarly, particular duties for particular protections are reasonable and more equitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty for general protection of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of trade in general has always been considered essential to the defence of the commonwealth and a necessary part of the duty of the executive power; collection and application of general customs duties have been left to that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between general protection (state responsibility) and particular branch protections (may be funded specially). Check consistency: if protection of a branch is part of general protection, state control is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate role for regulated companies vs joint-stock in providing protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular duties of protection have sometimes been entrusted to companies of merchants; these companies occasionally were useful for introducing branches of commerce but often proved burdensome, useless, mismanaged, or confinement-inducing in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether entrusting protection to private companies aligns incentives and delivers durable value. Regulated companies may be suitable for ministerial maintenance (moderate, limited expense); joint-stock are better for capital-intensive defenses (forts/garrisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and risks of regulated companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulated companies admit members on payment of a fine and submission to regulations; they resemble enlarged municipal monopolies, often subject to restrictive terms of admission and bye-laws that discourage new adventurers and confine trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect terms of admission, fines, age or residency restrictions, and bye-laws. Signs of monopoly: high or arbitrary fines, exclusionary membership rules, control over shipping/schedules that advantage insiders. Even if not currently oppressive, regulated companies tend toward uselessness or oppression without legal restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulated companies sometimes initially useful but harmful long-term
rubrics_metrics.description: Such companies may have been useful for first introduction of some branches of commerce by making experiments at their own expense, but in the long run they have universally proved either burdensome or useless, and have mismanaged or confined trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider time-horizon: temporary protective/regulatory arrangements might be justified to launch trade, but should be sunsetted or reformed to avoid long-term monopoly harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and trade-offs of joint-stock companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-stock companies share profit/loss in proportion to shares; shares are transferable; they attract more capital and adventurers by limiting individual liability, but directors manage other people's money and may neglect small matters causing negligence and profusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh greater capital and capacity (good for forts/garrisons, large undertakings) against weaker day-to-day vigilance by directors. Governance mechanisms and accountability (dividend scrutiny, proprietor engagement) are crucial to mitigate negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of exclusive privileges (charters) on company performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive privileges conferred by charters or acts of parliament commonly failed to prevent mismanagement; without exclusive privileges companies often could not compete, and with them they both mismanaged and confined trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize whether exclusivity is necessary and whether it produces net benefit or simply entrenches monopoly. Historical examples: Royal African company, South Sea company, Hudson's Bay company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and oversight for companies charged with public defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When companies are charged with maintenance of forts/garrisons or of public ministers, Parliament has sometimes allocated annual sums and required accounting, but oversight can be weak (parliament inattentive; auditors lacking specific expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess oversight structures: who audits accounts, whether auditors have relevant expertise, whether political bodies will actually scrutinize small recurring sums. Weak oversight risks poor application of funds (e.g., poor-quality materials shipped for fort repairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design to restrain monopoly within regulated companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal measures can limit monopolistic behaviour (e.g., reducing fines for admission, removing residency restrictions, granting appeals against bye-laws to board of trade or committee), but such remedies may be insufficient or limited by time windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for statutory remedies: appeals processes, limits on fines, removal of restrictive residency/merchant-only rules. Beware of short appeal windows and mechanisms that fail to remedy later-discovered pernicious bye-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance rules to reduce capture and abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices like limiting committee tenure (no more than three years), selection by diverse ports (London, Bristol, Liverpool), and ability to remove committeemen by board of trade were intended to reduce monopoly spirit and concentrate management accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governance constraints (term limits, election methods, removal authority) and whether they align decision-makers' incentives with public interest. Weak or self-interested governance invites favoritism and consignments to insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate allocation of public diplomatic/protective expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance of ambassadors and consuls is properly a state expense; companies often contributed historically, but state ought to bear such expenses to avoid distortion and unequal access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer state funding for diplomacy/public protection; company-funded ministers may create partiality or exclude broader merchant benefit. Consider whether company taxes for these services are redistributive or extractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation of interlopers or private adventurers to fund company defenses is distortionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to tax private adventurers (e.g., a 10% duty) to fund company maintenance often failed to restore company competitiveness and contributed to decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of policies that levy heavy duties on competitors to prop up companies — they may not restore competitiveness and can lead to company decline and eventual state intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational competence required for long-distance military works
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance of distant forts/garrisons requires managerial competence and appropriate material supply; mismanagement (e.g., sending poor-quality bricks and stones) undermines the purpose and wastes resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess logistical capabilities, choice of materials, and managerial accountability when entrusting long-distance maintenance to companies or committees. Parliamentary grants without effective oversight produce waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market effects of companies' restrictive conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies tend to keep markets 'understocked' to raise their own rate of profit and restrain competition — by discouraging new adventurers, imposing fines, or manipulating shipping schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for market indicators of under-supply, barriers to entry, or rules that favour insiders. Competitive entry by speculative adventurers is healthy and helps correct profit excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share transferability and liability as determinants of company scale and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In private copartneries partners cannot transfer shares and are bound for company debts to the whole extent of their fortune; in joint-stock companies shares are transferable and members are liable only to the extent of their share — this encourages more adventurers and larger aggregated capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how transferability and liability rules influence capital raising, risk appetite, and the pool of potential investors. Limited liability and liquidity attract larger pools but require stronger governance to control moral hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency principle between public duty and delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: If protection of a particular branch is truly part of the general protection of trade (a sovereign duty), it should remain under sovereign disposal; delegating such duties to private companies is inconsistent if nations claim general protection as a state responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for principled consistency: tasks considered public goods by the state should not be offloaded to private bodies without careful justification and safeguards.
